steps.instruction: Twelve people were split at random: six on a treatment, six on a placebo. **5 of 6** improved on the treatment, **2 of 6** on the placebo — a gap of \(5/6 - 2/6 = 0.50\).

gate.question: Suppose the treatment does nothing at all. Could a split of these same twelve people still produce a gap of 0.50?

choices.text: Yes — which six landed in each group is the only thing that changed
No — a gap that big can only come from a real effect
No — if the treatment does nothing the gap must be exactly 0

gate.feedback: If the treatment does nothing, each person's outcome would have been the same whichever group they were put in. So the same twelve cards could have been dealt differently — and some deals produce a gap.

steps.instruction: Press **+1** a few times. Each press deals the *same twelve outcomes* into two new groups of six.
steps.observe: Watch the cards move. Does any card ever change from improved to not improved?
steps.reveal: Never. The outcomes are fixed; only the grouping changes. That is the whole idea of a randomization test — it asks what the gap would look like if the labels meant nothing, and the only honest way to answer is to re-deal the labels.

requires.hint: Press **+10** until you have at least 50 — you have {{trials}}.

steps.observe: The pile is made of **spikes**, not bars. Why only six of them?
steps.reveal: With six in each group and seven improvements in all, the treatment group can contain 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 of them — six possibilities, and no others. The gap can only be \(\pm 5/6\), \(\pm 1/2\) or \(\pm 1/6\). There is nothing in between to draw.

steps.observe: The two middle spikes are much taller than the rest. Why would chance favour a small gap?
steps.reveal: There are far more ways to deal the seven improvements evenly than to pile them into one group. Three-and-four can happen 350 ways out of 924; six-and-one only 7. The shape of the pile is a counting fact, not a property of the treatment.

steps.instruction: The observed gap, 0.50, is marked on the pile, with everything at least that big shaded.

gate.question: Among your {{trials}} shuffles — all of them produced by chance alone — how unusual is a gap of 0.50?

choices.text: Not very — chance produces a gap that big fairly often
Very — almost no shuffle reached it

gate.feedback: About one shuffle in eight. Dealing all 924 possible ways gives 112 of them, or 0.121 — so a gap this size is an ordinary result of shuffling, and these data give little reason to credit the treatment.

prompts.label: In your own words
prompts.placeholder: The shaded share counts the shuffles that…

steps.reveal: The shaded share is the p-value: the fraction of re-deals — made under the assumption that the treatment does nothing — that produce a gap at least as large as the one actually seen. Here that is about 0.12, which is common enough that chance is a comfortable explanation. ⚠ That is not proof the treatment does nothing. Twelve people is very little evidence either way.
